simple: The interest rate at which a central bank lends money to banks.
example: When the RBI raises it, loans usually get costlier for everyone.

simple: How fast prices of everyday things go up.
example: 5% inflation means something worth ₹100 last year costs about ₹105 now.

simple: The total value of everything a country produces in a year.
example: GDP growing means the economy is getting bigger.

simple: A small piece of ownership in a company.
example: Own 1 share of a company and you own a tiny part of it.

simple: Scores that track India's biggest companies on the stock market.
example: Sensex up means those big companies' shares rose on average.

simple: A long period when share prices keep rising.
example: Think of a bull pushing its horns upward.

simple: A period when share prices fall 20% or more from their peak.
example: Think of a bear swiping its paws downward.

simple: The first time a company sells its shares to the public.
example: After its IPO, anyone can buy the company's shares.

simple: A share of profits a company pays to its shareholders.
example: A ₹5 dividend pays you ₹5 for every share you own.

simple: A company's total value on the stock market.
example: Share price × number of shares = market cap.

simple: A loan you give to a government or company that pays you interest.
example: Buy a government bond and the government pays you back with interest.

simple: The yearly return you earn from a bond.
example: When bond prices fall, their yields go up.

simple: When a country's economy shrinks for a sustained period.
example: Often means fewer jobs and less spending.

simple: When a government spends more than it earns.
example: The gap is usually covered by borrowing.

simple: How a central bank controls money supply and interest rates.
example: The RBI and the US Fed set monetary policy.

simple: The bank that manages a country's money, like RBI in India or the Fed in the US.
example: It sets interest rates and prints currency.

simple: How much one currency is worth in another.
example: If $1 = ₹84, you need ₹84 to buy one dollar.

simple: When the rupee buys less foreign currency than before.
example: Imports like petrol and phones can get costlier.

simple: A digital currency that isn't controlled by any government or bank.
example: Its price can swing a lot in a single day.

simple: A cryptocurrency designed to keep a steady value, usually $1.
example: USDT and USDC aim to always equal one US dollar.

simple: A shared digital record book that no one can secretly edit.
example: Cryptocurrencies record every transaction on one.

simple: A pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager.
example: Your ₹500 joins lakhs of others' money in one fund.

simple: Investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund every month.
example: ₹1,000 every month, automatically.

simple: A fund that trades on the stock market like a single share.
example: A Nifty ETF lets you buy all 50 Nifty companies in one go.

simple: How much and how fast a price moves up and down.
example: High volatility means big swings.

simple: How easily something can be turned into cash.
example: Cash is very liquid; a house is not.

simple: A tax a country puts on goods imported from other countries.
example: Tariffs can make foreign products costlier for buyers.

simple: When a country imports more than it exports.
example: India imports more oil than it sells abroad.

simple: Foreign investors buying or selling shares in a country's market.
example: Big FII selling can pull Indian markets down.

simple: India's stock market regulator, like a referee for investors.
example: It makes rules to protect people who invest.

simple: The US central bank, the Federal Reserve.
example: Its rate decisions move markets worldwide, including India.

simple: Consumer Price Index: a measure of how prices of everyday goods change.
example: It's the main number used to measure inflation.

simple: A company's profit over a period, usually a quarter.
example: Companies report earnings every three months.

simple: All the money a company brings in from sales, before costs.
example: Revenue minus costs = profit.

simple: Share price divided by the profit per share.
example: A high P/E means investors pay more for each rupee of profit.

simple: Betting that a share's price will fall.
example: Sell borrowed shares now, buy them back later hopefully cheaper.

simple: An automatic pause in trading when prices move too far too fast.
example: It gives the market time to calm down.

simple: Raw, unrefined oil, priced worldwide in dollars.
example: When it gets costlier, petrol and transport prices tend to rise.

simple: Gold a central bank keeps as a safety store of value.
example: Countries hold gold to back confidence in their money.

simple: Foreign currencies a country's central bank keeps in stock.
example: They help steady the rupee and pay for imports.

simple: High inflation and a slow economy at the same time.
example: Prices rise while jobs and growth stay weak.

simple: A central bank buying bonds to push more money into the economy.
example: Used when cutting interest rates isn't enough.

simple: A grade showing how likely a borrower is to repay debt.
example: AAA is the highest; lower grades mean more risk.

simple: When a borrower fails to repay a loan on time.
example: A country defaulting can shake global markets.

simple: A single number tracking a group of stocks.
example: S&P 500, Nifty 50 and FTSE 100 are indexes.

simple: All the investments a person owns together.
example: Stocks, gold and mutual funds in one basket.

simple: Spreading money across different investments to lower risk.
example: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.

simple: Earning interest on your interest too.
example: Money grows faster the longer you leave it.

simple: Goods and Services Tax, India's main tax on things you buy.
example: It's included in the price you pay at shops.

simple: A government's yearly plan for how it will earn and spend money.
example: India's Union Budget is presented every February.
